segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “When evening comes, you say, ‘Fair weather, for the sky is red,’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and in the morning, ‘Stormy today, for the sky is red and overcast.’ You know how to interpret the face of the sky, but the signs of the times you cannot.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he left them and went away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Watch out, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They began discussing this among themselves, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We didn’t bring any bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Aware of this, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves that you brought no bread?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do you not yet understand? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many large baskets you gathered?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: How do you not understand that I was not speaking to you about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven in bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus came to the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and still others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “But you—who do you say I am?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon Peter answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And I in turn tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not overpower it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of the heavens, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in the heavens, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in the heavens.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he gave the disciples strict orders to tell no one that he was the Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From then on Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “God forbid, Lord! This will never happen to you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he turned and said to Peter,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, because your mind is not on the things of God but on the things of people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If anyone wants to come after me, let them deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake will find it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For what will it profit a person if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life? Or what will a person give in exchange for their life?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to what they have done.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”

notes.note: The older English tradition has “tempting,” but the Greek verb means to put someone to the test, here with hostile intent. Modern English “tempt” has narrowed to enticing someone to sin, which is not the point. Most modern translations also use “test” in this verse.

The weather saying, from these words to the end of verse 3, is absent from several important early manuscripts, and some scholars think it was added later under the influence of Luke 12:54–56. Others think it is original and was dropped by copyists in regions such as Egypt, where a red morning sky does not signal rain. The edition translated here prints the words without brackets.

Jesus has already explained this phrase at 12:39–40, where Jonah’s three days in the sea creature point to the Son of Man’s three days in the earth. “Adulterous” follows the prophets’ image of Israel’s unfaithfulness to God as marital infidelity. It is not a charge of sexual misconduct.

The Greek word translates the Hebrew for “anointed one,” the king Israel was expecting. Here it is a title under discussion, not a name, so “Messiah” conveys what Peter’s hearers would have understood. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it works as a name.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 19, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses constantly. Most translations flatten it to “heaven.” The plural is kept here so that the reader hears what a first-century hearer heard.

notes.phrase: you are Peter, and on this rock
notes.note: The Greek plays on the name Peter (Petros) and the word for rock (petra); in Aramaic both would probably be the single word kepha. Whether “this rock” is Peter himself, his confession, or Jesus has been debated since antiquity. Most modern scholars across traditions take it to be Peter in his role as the one who confesses, but the question is not settled.

The nearly universal rendering is “church,” and readers know what it refers to. A first-century hearer, however, knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament’s term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so “assembly” is used throughout this translation.

Hades is the realm of the dead, not the place of final punishment. “The gates of Hades” is an Old Testament expression for death (compare Isaiah 38:10). The most common reading is that death will not overcome the community Jesus builds, though some take the gates as an image of hostile powers.

notes.phrase: will be bound in the heavens
notes.note: The Greek construction can also be rendered “will have been bound,” which would mean that Peter’s decisions follow what heaven has already determined, not that heaven ratifies them. Grammarians are divided on whether the form carries that force here. “Bind” and “loose” were used in Jewish teaching for forbidding and permitting, and perhaps also for excluding from and readmitting to the community.

notes.traditional: Be it far from thee, Lord
notes.note: The Greek is literally “merciful to you,” a compressed idiom from the Greek Old Testament. It is usually understood as “May God be merciful to you,” that is, “God forbid.” Some take it more mildly as “Mercy on you, Lord.” Either way it is a strong exclamation rejecting what has just been said.

Many translations switch from “life” in verse 25 to “soul” here, but the Greek word is the same in both verses, and the argument depends on it. In first-century usage the word most often means a person’s life or living self, not an immaterial part of them. Some translations, such as the NRSV, also keep “life” throughout.

What event this saying points to is disputed. Proposals include the transfiguration that follows immediately, the resurrection and the spread of the gospel, the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, and the final return of the Son of Man. The translation leaves the wording as open as the Greek.

candidates.reason: Translations split between “leaven” and “yeast”; the word recurs in the Gospels and Paul as a fixed metaphor and should be one English word throughout.
Rendered variously as “scribes,” “teachers of the law,” or “experts in the law”; it is frequent across the Gospels and Acts and needs one consistent choice.
A distinctive address recurring in Matthew and Luke that should be worded identically wherever it appears.
Used of rebuking people, demons, and wind, and also for giving a stern warning; translators vary between “rebuke,” “warn,” and “sternly order.”
“This generation” sayings recur across the Gospels, and whether the word means contemporaries, a kind of people, or an age affects several disputed passages.
